section_summary: This section consists of forty-nine separate copies of a petition addressed to the President of the United States and Congress concerning the Japanese invasion of China. The petition condemns civilian bombing and other destruction, invokes the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact, and asks the United States to halt exports of aircraft, shells, scrap iron, oil, trucks, and other war materials to Japan. Many copies bear individual signatures, addresses, or church affiliations, principally from the Washington, D.C.–Maryland area, though numerous handwritten entries are poorly represented by the OCR.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by W. Eastman
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests action to end American traffic in materials supporting Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japanese aggression, civilian bombing, and destruction in China while invoking the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact. This copy is signed by W. Eastman and gives a La Verre Avenue address.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. Mary Fincher
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests action to end American traffic in materials supporting Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition asks the United States to stop exports of aircraft, shells, scrap iron, oil, trucks, and similar supplies to Japan. The OCR appears to identify the signer as Mrs. Mary Fincher, at a Connecticut Avenue address.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Fnta Hiclhdle
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges the federal government to stop American commerce that sustains Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition links American exports to Japan’s bombing and destruction of Chinese civilian communities. The handwritten signer’s name is poorly rendered as “Fnta Hiclhdle,” with a Connecticut Avenue address and an apparent Baptist church affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. Rachel Crane
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for direct or indirect measures to end American material support for Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: The petition describes Japan as an aggressor and treaty violator and expresses support for an independent, democratic China. This copy appears to be signed by Mrs. Rachel Crane.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mary Riley Orben
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Seeks an end to exports from the United States that facilitate Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition protests civilian casualties and the destruction of schools, churches, hospitals, and businesses in China. The signer’s name appears in uncertain OCR as Mary Riley Orben.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Massie Lyons
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Asks the President and Congress to stop American supplies from contributing to destruction in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that American raw materials, planes, shells, oil, and trucks make the United States a partner in Japanese aggression. This copy appears to be signed by Massie Lyons of Chesapeake Street.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. Gould Wickey
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges measures against the shipment of American strategic materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japanese attacks upon Chinese civilians and institutions and asks that supporting trade be ended. The signer appears to be Mrs. Gould Wickey, though the handwritten entry is uncertain.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. Helen Bacchus
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests an end to American exports used by Japan in its invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition cites international lawlessness, treaty violations, and the use of American materials in Japanese weapons. The signature is tentatively read as Mrs. Helen Bacchus.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Naomi B. Lyons
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for the United States to cease commerce assisting Japanese military operations.
subfiles.summary: The petition supports Chinese independence and condemns profits derived from Japanese destruction of civilians. This copy is apparently signed by Naomi B. Lyons.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. M. L. Bennett
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Seeks federal action to stop American supplies from sustaining Japan’s invasion.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns bombing and the supply of American raw materials and military-use goods to Japan. The signature appears to read Mrs. M. L. Bennett, with a Washington, D.C., address.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Lucia S. Shant
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests measures to end American commerce contributing to Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that continued exports make Americans complicit in the destruction of the Chinese people. Lucia S. Shant signs this copy and records a 20th Street address and Mount Pleasant Congregational affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. A. Larkin
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to exports of materials used by Japan against China.
subfiles.summary: The petition protests Japanese aggression and American commercial participation in the war. The handwritten signature is tentatively read as Mrs. A. Larkin.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Delia M. Orcutt
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges the President and Congress to halt American trade supporting Japan’s invasion.
subfiles.summary: The petition lists scrap iron, oil, trucks, planes, and shells among the American goods aiding the Japanese war effort. This copy is signed by Mrs. Delia M. Orcutt of Mount Rainier, Maryland.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by A. Abernethy
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests that the United States stop traffic in materials furthering the war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition invokes peace, treaty obligations, and concern for Chinese civilians. The OCR of the signature is highly uncertain but may identify A. Abernethy, with a Calvary Baptist Church affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Harriet Guch
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for American measures against commerce that supports Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns the destruction of Chinese civilian life and institutions with weapons and materials supplied from America. The signature is tentatively read as Harriet Guch and is accompanied by a University Place address.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China with illegible signature
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests an end to American traffic in goods that support the Japanese war effort.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japan’s invasion and the use of American planes, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks. A signature mark is present, but the OCR does not preserve an identifiable name.

subfiles.title: Unsigned petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges the federal government to end American material support for Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition charges Japan with aggression and treaty violations and condemns the bombing of Chinese cities. No signer or address is visible in the OCR copy.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Lily Slasr Teux
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to exports that make Americans partners in Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The petition supports the Chinese people’s effort to build an independent democratic state and protests American trade with Japan. The handwritten signer’s name is poorly represented as Lily Slasr Teux.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Florence Wright
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Seeks direct or indirect action to halt American supplies for Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: The petition describes Japanese aggression and the destruction of Chinese civilian communities and institutions. Florence Wright signs this copy and gives a Massachusetts Avenue address.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China with illegible signature
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests that the United States end commercial support for Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition protests Japan’s conduct and the shipment of American military-use goods. The OCR captures only an illegible signature trace, so the petitioner cannot be identified.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. Alice O. Farmer
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for measures to end American traffic in materials used by Japan in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns civilian bombing and American commercial involvement in Japanese aggression. The signature is tentatively read as Mrs. Alice O. Farmer, apparently of Kensington, Maryland.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Anna N. Schroeder
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges an end to American exports that further Japan’s war against China.
subfiles.summary: The petition identifies planes, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks as goods contributing to the Japanese war effort. The handwritten signature is tentatively read as Anna N. Schroeder and includes an 11th Street address.

subfiles.title: Unsigned petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests federal action to stop American materials from supporting Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The petition declares that continued trade makes the United States complicit in the destruction of the Chinese people. No signature or identifying information is visible on this copy.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by S. D. Torche
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for the cessation of American commerce furthering Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japanese treaty violations and attacks upon Chinese civilians and institutions. The OCR gives the signer uncertainly as S. D. Torche, with a Washington address and Methodist affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. S. E. Braden
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Asks the President and Congress to end American material support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that American planes, shells, oil, scrap iron, and trucks facilitate destruction in China. The signature is tentatively read as Mrs. S. E. Braden.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Miss Stevenson
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests action to end American traffic in goods supporting Japan’s invasion.
subfiles.summary: The petition protests Japan’s attacks on civilians and seeks support for an independent, democratic China. The OCR preserves only an uncertain surname, Stevenson, together with an apparent Presbyterian affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. H. E. Yalland
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges federal measures to halt American supplies for the Japanese war effort.
subfiles.summary: The petition invokes the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact while condemning bombing and civilian destruction. The signer appears to be Mrs. H. E. Yalland of Bethesda, Maryland, with a Bethesda Presbyterian affiliation.

subfiles.title: Unsigned petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to American trade contributing to Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns the use of American materials in Japan’s war and expresses solidarity with the Chinese people. A signature line is present, but no name is captured.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. Walter Crawford
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests action to prevent American commerce from supporting Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: The petition protests Japanese aggression and asks that exports of war-related supplies be stopped. The poorly recognized signature may read Mrs. Walter Crawford and is accompanied by an apparent St. Paul Methodist affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China from an unidentified signatory
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for measures to stop American materials from aiding Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns civilian bombing and commercial profit from Japanese aggression. No personal name is legible, although an address and an apparent Reformed church affiliation are recorded.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Dudley McCarrens
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Seeks an end to American commerce that facilitates Japan’s destruction in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition presents American exports as enabling Japanese bombing, killing, and destruction. The handwritten signature is tentatively read as Dudley McCarrens.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Eva B. McNair
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges the United States to stop supplying materials used in Japan’s war against China.
subfiles.summary: The petition calls for direct or indirect action against traffic in war materials and supports Chinese independence. Eva B. McNair appears to sign this copy, which includes a Takoma Park Baptist affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Jarrel Kouran
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests that American exports sustaining Japanese aggression be ended.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japanese attacks on Chinese civilians and the shipment of strategic goods from the United States. The name is uncertainly read as Jarrel Kouran, with an apparent First Christian affiliation in Alexandria, Virginia.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Be ingd 9. Baroved
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to American material assistance to Japan’s war effort.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that American trade contributes to the destruction of Chinese civilians and institutions. The signer’s name is illegible in the OCR, which renders it as “Be ingd 9. Baroved,” followed by a Methodist church reference.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Edna H. Edgington
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges measures to stop American goods from contributing to the war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japanese aggression and the commercial traffic supplying its armed forces. The signature is tentatively reconstructed as Edna H. Edgington, with an additional location or affiliation that remains illegible.

subfiles.title: Unsigned petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests an end to American exports used by Japan against China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns treaty violations, bombing, and the destruction of civilian institutions. The word “Signed” appears, but the OCR contains no corresponding personal name.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mary P. Cullough
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls upon the President and Congress to halt commerce supporting Japan’s invasion.
subfiles.summary: The petition opposes American participation in the destruction of the Chinese people through trade in war materials. The signature is tentatively read as Mary P. Cullough and is accompanied by a Tuckerman Street address.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mary S. Radford
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges the federal government to stop American materials from aiding Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japanese aggression and the bombing and killing of Chinese civilians. The poorly recognized signature appears to be Mary S. Radford, with a 34th Street address.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. Annie Ferguson
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests action to end American traffic in supplies for the Japanese war effort.
subfiles.summary: The petition lists American aircraft, shells, scrap iron, oil, and trucks as contributions to the war in China. The signature is tentatively read as Mrs. Annie Ferguson.

subfiles.title: Unsigned petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for direct or indirect measures to halt American support for Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japan’s invasion and supports the Chinese people’s pursuit of an independent democratic state. No signer’s name or other identifying entry is present in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mrs. Chas. O. Patterson
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges an end to American commerce that supports Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition protests civilian destruction and American exports of military-use goods. Mrs. Chas. O. Patterson signs this copy, giving a Sheridan Street address in Washington, D.C., and an apparent Emory Methodist affiliation.

subfiles.title: Unsigned petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests that the United States halt trade facilitating the Japanese invasion.
subfiles.summary: The petition argues that American raw materials and manufactured goods sustain Japanese violence in China. The signature area contains only “Signed,” without an identifiable name.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Agnes Foennten
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to American traffic in materials used against the Chinese people.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japan’s invasion and asks the President and Congress to act under the principle of the Good Neighbor. The signer’s name is rendered uncertainly as Agnes Foennten.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Frances Rubb
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges measures to stop American goods from sustaining Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The petition denounces bombing and destruction in China and asks for an end to related American commerce. The signature is tentatively read as Frances Rubb, with a Randolph address and Calvary Baptist Church affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mahon
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests that American trade contributing to Japan’s war in China be ended.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japan as an aggressor and protests the use of American supplies in its military campaign. A brief handwritten entry, uncertainly read as “Mahon,” appears beneath the signature line.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Mabel R. Harding
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls upon the President and Congress to halt exports furthering the Japanese invasion.
subfiles.summary: The petition links American trade to the killing of Chinese civilians and the destruction of institutions. The signature appears to be Mabel R. Harding, with an Underwood Street address and Methodist affiliation.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Motherhead
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Seeks an end to American material support for Japan’s aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition invokes international law and urges action against shipments of strategic materials. The OCR renders the signer’s name uncertainly as “Motherhead,” with a partially legible address.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese invasion of China signed by Louise L. Merrell
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests federal action to end American commerce assisting Japan’s war effort.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japanese bombing and destruction and argues that American exporters are profiting from aggression. Louise L. Merrell signs this copy and gives an address at the Wyoming Apartments.

subfiles.title: Unsigned petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to American traffic in goods contributing to Japan’s destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition asks the President and Congress to use every practicable direct or indirect means to end the trade. The signature area contains no identifiable name in the OCR.
